newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Russia-NATO row hangs over European summit.
newsitem.headline: Russia-NATO row hangs over European summit.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
A European security summit hoping to lay the foundations of peace for the 21st century opens on Monday, but with another row looming between Russia and the West over NATO expansion.

Leaders from the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) will approve plans for shoring up peace in Bosnia, set a new course for arms control and discuss problems such as the crisis in Belarus at the two-day summit.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is expected to underline Moscow's opposition to plans for the Western alliance to take in new members from Eastern Europe -- an issue which has already disrupted efforts to build a new age of cooperation in the post-Cold War world.
"We are categorically against the expansion of NATO to the East," Chernomyrdin said as he left Moscow for Lisbon. "Russia has its position and will stand by it at the OSCE meeting."
President Boris Yeltsin, recovering from heart surgery, is not coming to the summit and has sent Chernomyrdin instead.

Yeltsin also took a tough line against NATO last week, saying expanding the alliance would lead to "new divisions in Europe". Russia says it will be isolated and threatened if countries like Poland and Hungary join the Western alliance.
Western diplomats say they would prefer the Lisbon summit, which brings together the United States and Canada with all European states, to avoid the debate on NATO enlargement.
The last OSCE summit two years ago in Budapest was wrecked by a row over the same issue and differences over Bosnia.
Leaders will issue a declaration in Lisbon committing all countries to work together in search of peace and to develop a security blueprint so that no nation will feel threatened.

Russia has found little support for its efforts to go further and develop the OSCE into a more powerful institution that would act as a counterbalance to NATO. Moscow has insisted the summit must not appear to endorse the alliance's plans.
Russia wants to create a pan-European security system which is free of blocs and divisions, guarantees equal security to all participants and controls arms levels on the continent.

Western nations, and Eastern European countries which are queuing up to join NATO, oppose any measures which would limit their freedom. The United States, which will be represented by Vice President Al Gore, has taken a tough line on this.
Diplomats said the summit declaration would endorse the general right of countries to join alliances, but without mentioning NATO so as to avoid any direct offence to Moscow.
One year after the end of the war in Bosnia, the meeting will agree a continued role for the OSCE there over the next two years, working in parallel with the NATO-led peace force.

The OSCE has taken a major role in implementing the Bosnian peace agreement, organising September's elections, overseeing an arms control agreement for former Yugoslavia and monitoring human rights and democratic freedoms in the region.
Bosnia and Croatia will attend but the rump Yugoslav state of Serbia and Montenegro was suspended from the OSCE in 1992.

Leaders will also agree that a new round of arms talks should start in Vienna next year to cut military hardware in Europe, adapting and expanding a 1990 treaty signed between NATO and the now-defunct Warsaw Pact.
Russia has insisted the treaty should be adapted to reflect the new security situation and the West hopes this will go some way to reassuring Moscow that NATO does not pose a threat.

Many leaders are expected to voice concern about developments in Belarus, where President Alexander Lukashenko has strengthened his grip on power in a recent referendum. The OSCE said on Saturday it was seriously concerned by the problems with democracy in the former Soviet republic.

Since its birth in 1975 in Helsinki as an East-West forum for discussing issues from democracy to economics, the security forum has played a key role in bringing about arms reductions, organising ballots and giving early warning of potential ethnic conflicts in Europe. REUTER
